extracted.intended_audience: inventors, engineers, manufacturers, and students of mechanical arts
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for evaluating or designing machines and tools — focusing on economy of time, use of materials, power generation/transmission, regulation, velocity management, power accumulation, and accelerating natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of time (use of methods that drastically reduce labour time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer methods or devices that save large amounts of labour/time even if they require small consumable expense or present initial difficulty; examples include using gunpowder to blast rock and improved diamond mounts to shorten apprenticeship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate inventions by how much human labour/time they save in practice. Example: a few pounds of gunpowder (cheap) can achieve in minutes what best tools could not in many months; an improved diamond mounting allows novices to cut glass reliably, saving years of apprenticeship and destroyed material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment of low-value or waste materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of by-products or otherwise low-value materials for productive purposes (turning refuse into useful inputs) is an advantage of mechanical/chemical processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a process or machine makes profitable use of 'offal' or scrap (e.g., skins for goldbeating, hoofs for chemical salts, worn tin cut and varnished for trunk-maker edges, worn iron used by chemists). Consider lifecycle value extraction and supply-chain effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate distinction and use of tools versus machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when a simple hand tool is preferable and when a framed, powered machine is appropriate; tools are generally simpler and hand-operated, while machines transmit or generate power (animal/steam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design or evaluate devices by their intended complexity and power source. Simple tasks may be best served by cheap, elegant tools; more complex or powered tasks by machines that integrate tools into frames driven by external power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design simple, inexpensive contrivances for repetitive tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, inexpensive tools that exploit object geometry and motion (e.g., concave tray for aligning needles; finger-stall method for sorting needles) can transform tedious processes into rapid ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a process, look for simple mechanical contrivances that convert an otherwise slow, manual repetition into a rapid, repeatable action. Examples and anti-patterns: trays that use shaking and shape to align needles; finger-stall that sorts multiple needles per motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of additional limbs or hands by mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines that substitute for an extra hand (treadle-operated dies, vices, clamps) enable a single worker to perform multi-handed operations or avoid reheating/extra steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the device reduces the need for multiple simultaneous operator actions (e.g., nail-maker using foot treadle to operate a die and free hands). Consider reductions in cycle count, reheating, and necessary personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of machinery to enable handicapped persons to work
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs that allow persons deprived of limbs or senses to perform work (e.g., shoe machinery, weaving machines for the blind) are socially valuable advantages of mechanical invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value inventions that increase accessibility and allow precise operation despite physical disabilities. Examples: machines enabling blind persons to weave sash-lines; tooling that compensates for loss of an arm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of machinery purposes: produce power vs transmit/execute work
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines can be classified into (1) those employed to produce power, and (2) those intended to transmit force and execute work; this classification matters in design and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a machine, identify whether its primary role is power generation (e.g., wind, water, steam) or force transmission/execution (e.g., levers, pulleys). Different design considerations and limits apply to each class.

rubrics_metrics.name: No creation of power by mechanical combinations (conservation principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical contrivances cannot create power; levers, pulleys, wedges, etc., only transmit or change direction/rapidity of motion, with losses from friction and other causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of 'gaining power' critically — designs can improve speed/effectiveness but cannot increase total power beyond input. Consider frictional losses and the necessity of additional force when increasing rapidity of execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between force and time (optimize time even if power increases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations of mechanical art augment force at the expense of time or vice versa; often initial methods are far from optimal and significant gains are possible by changing tools (e.g., hatchet → saw → wedge → gunpowder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a new device meaningfully reduces time to perform a task, even if it requires a different allocation of force or consumables. Historical examples (saw, wedge, gunpowder) illustrate progressive improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of transport and material handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical methods and packing/separation techniques that reduce transported bulk/weight (e.g., removing cotton seed before shipping, compact packing) substantially lower transport costs and should be considered advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inventions for their impact on logistics and handling: does the process reduce unnecessary transported weight/volume? Consider comparative packaging and pre-processing effects on freight cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulating or storing power for intermittent high-force needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use devices that accumulate energy (fly-wheels, raised weights, heavy rims) so a modest continuous input can supply brief bursts of much greater power when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mechanisms for their ability to store kinetic or potential energy and release it in concentrated form (fly-wheels spun ahead of heavy rolling; lifting weights and allowing them to fall; timing engine start to charge fly-wheel). Consider required lead time and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulating power and ensuring uniformity/steadiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical governors, vanes, cataracts, fuel-supply hoppers, and dampers provide uniform and safe operating rates, reduce wear, and economize fuel; regulation is essential where increased speed is dangerous or wasteful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess control systems for speed/fuel regulation and their responsiveness. Examples: Watt governor for steam engines, vanes/fly for small mechanisms, adjustable hopper-fed fuel supply that reduces smoke and saves coal, cataract timing device for steam stroke regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching velocity to human fatigue and task requirements (increase/diminution of velocity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimize the speed (velocity and frequency) of operations to balance muscular fatigue, tool motion, and production rate — increasing velocity for light repetitive work and diminishing it to overcome heavy resistance with limited power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ergonomics and cycle frequency: consider human fatigue (frequency vs force), modify tools to combine motions (e.g., shears bending tags while cutting), use gearing to increase thread/spindle speed, or use systems of pulleys/cranes to trade velocity for force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending the time of action of forces (retaining small input to act over long duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms (springs, trains of wheels, jacks) that distribute a small input over a long time (watches, clocks, meat-jacks, automatons) multiply the effective utility of brief human effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess devices by how effectively they transform a short input into prolonged action and whether the duration/consistency delivered suits the application (e.g., 24-hour watch from a short winding, jacks for slow roasting, spring-driven experimental apparatus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using mechanical methods to accelerate natural or slow chemical processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply mechanical principles (vacuum, pressure injection) to speed processes that are naturally slow (example: tanning hides by exhausting air then forcing tan solution into skins, reducing months/years to weeks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating processes that rely on natural diffusion/penetration, look for mechanical aids that change boundary conditions (evacuating entrapped air, applying pressure) to drastically reduce processing time; ensure vessel strength and process control for safety and quality.
